MEDICAL EDUCATION 2010;44: 85–93 85 INTRODUCTION Cognitive load theory (CLT) was initially developed in the 1980s. 1 By means of strictly controlled exper- imental studies, it aimed to develop instructional design principles and strategies based on a model of human cognitive architecture. Right from the start, CLT provided instructional design principles that were seen as counterintuitive by many practitioners in the ﬁeld of education. For example, the recom- mendation to provide novice learners with many worked examples rather than problems to solve contradicted the prevailing opinion of the time that solving problems was the best way to learn to solve problems. The theory has developed substantially since the 1980s (see reviews 2,3). Having established a variety of basic instructional designs that prevented the application of cognitive resources to unnecessary aspects of a task, an increasing number of cognitive load theorists from around the world considered how to deal with highly complex learning tasks, how to stimulate learners to actually use available cognitive resources for learning, and how to deal with the growing expertise of learners in educational programmes of longer duration. Applications of CLT in medical education are beginning to appear. 4,5 Moreover, educational approaches in the health professions increasingly stress the use of authentic tasks, which are expected to help students integrate the knowledge, skills and attitudes necessary for effective task performance in professional life. 6 Authentic learning tasks designed on the basis of real-life tasks have many different solutions, are ecologically valid and usually cannot be mastered in a single session. Whereas CLT may not be relevant to teaching simple tasks, it is critical when complex learning tasks are used because they impose a high load on the learner’s cognitive system. 7,8 Therefore, this article argues that design guidelines based on CLT are highly relevant to teaching in complex domains like the health professions, espe- cially when authentic learning tasks are part of the curriculum. The article brieﬂy presents, in order, the cognitive architecture assumed by CLT, the main design principles and strategies based on this archi- tecture, and a discussion of the presented framework. COGNITIVE ARCHITECTURE Cognitive load theory assumes a cognitive architec- ture that is broadly supported by research in cognitive psychology and can be explained readily from an evolutionary perspective. 9 This section brieﬂy summarises the theory in terms of memory systems, learning processes supported by those systems, and associated types of cognitive load. Memory systems Cognitive load theory assumes that the human cognitive system has a limited working memory that can hold no more than ﬁve to nine information elements (the famous ‘seven plus or minus two

Memory systems Cognitive load theory assumes that the human cognitive system has a limited working memory that can hold no more than ﬁve to nine information elements (the famous ‘seven plus or minus two’) 10 and actively process no more than two to four elements simultaneously. It is able to deal with information for no more than a few seconds and almost all information is lost after about 20 seconds unless it is refreshed by rehearsal. The theory emphasises that these working memory capacity and duration limitations only apply to novel information obtained through sensory memory. Working memory has no known limitations when dealing with infor- mation retrieved from long-term memory. In effect, long-term memory alters the characteristics of work- ing memory. Long-term memory holds cognitive schemas that vary in their degree of complexity and automation. Human expertise comes from knowl- edge organised by these schemas, not from an ability to engage in reasoning with many elements that have not been organised in long-term memory. Human working memory simply is not able to process many elements. Expertise develops as learners mindfully combine simple ideas into more complex ones. A medical student, for example, gradually combines simple ideas about consequences, enabling conditions and faults into so-called ‘illness scripts’, a term that describes a particular type of schema which allows the user to distinguish between alike diseases. Illness scripts can be interpreted during problem solving and reasoning and so help to reach an accurate diagnosis. These schemas organise knowledge but also heavily reduce working memory load because even a highly complex schema can be dealt with as one element in working memory. Fully automated schemas are developed as a function of extensive practice and can act as a central executive, organising information or knowledge that needs to be processed in working memory. Under these circumstances there are no limits to working memory. For instance, an experienced medical doc- tor recognises a ’warm shock’ resulting from redis- tribution of cardiac output at a single glance. Thus, for a novice student, a patient with a warm shock may show little more than an unstructured set of symptoms. Learning processes Working memory must inevitably be limited in capacity when dealing with completely novel, unor- ganised information because, as the number of elements that need to be organised increases linearly, the number of possible combinations of elements that must be tested for effectiveness during problem solving increases exponentially. Random testing of the effectiveness of possible combinations based on many elements becomes effectively impossible be- cause of a combinatorial explosion. This problem of exponential growth can only be accommodated by severely limiting the number of information units that are processed simultaneously. This is what learning processes such as schema construction and schema automation do by organising information in long-term memory. Schemas can be constructed during the problem-solving process by bringing elements together (i.e. chunking), by incorporating new elements in schemas already available in long- term memory or, more commonly, by obtaining already schematised information from other people. Schemas can then be treated as a single element in working memory and thus heavily decrease cognitive load associated with the performance of later tasks. Constructed schemas may become automated if they are repeatedly applied and yield desired results. As is the case for schema construction, automation can free working memory capacity for other activities because an automated schema, acting as a central executive, directly steers behaviour without needing to process it in working memory. Because automation requires a great deal of practice, automated schemas only develop for those aspects of performance that are consistent across task situations, such as routines for operating medical equipment and standard pro- cedures for using software applications. Thus, from an instructional design perspective, well-designed instruction should not only encourage schema construction, but should also support schema automation for those aspects that are consistent across tasks. 6,11 Types of cognitive load Novel information must be processed in working memory in order to construct schemas in long-term memory. The ease with which information may be processed in working memory is a focus of CLT. Working memory load may be affected by the intrinsic nature of the learning tasks (intrinsic load), by the manner in which the tasks are presented (extraneous load), and by the learning that actually occurs (germane load) when dealing with intrinsic load. Intrinsic load cannot be altered by instructional interventions without altering the task to be learned (e.g. simpliﬁcation)

Working memory load may be affected by the intrinsic nature of the learning tasks (intrinsic load), by the manner in which the tasks are presented (extraneous load), and by the learning that actually occurs (germane load) when dealing with intrinsic load. Intrinsic load cannot be altered by instructional interventions without altering the task to be learned (e.g. simpliﬁcation) or by the act of learning itself. It depends on the number of elements that must be processed simultaneously in working memory, a number which, in turn, depends on the extent of element interactivity of the materials or tasks that must be learned. Element interactivity is the degree to which the elements of something to be learned can, or cannot, be understood in isolation. For example, vocabulary is an example of low element-interactive material in the ﬁeld of language learning. Although there are thousands of words to be learned, most people can quickly learn some simple words because words may be learned in isolation from all other words. Grammar, by contrast, is an example of high element-interactive material. Most people have difﬁ- culty in generating grammatically correct sentences, even when all the words to be used in the sentence are known. This is because many elements must be considered simultaneously; that is, to build sentences that are grammatically correct, one must attend to all the words within the sentence at once while also considering syntax, tense and verb endings. Tasks with high element interactivity are difﬁcult to understand and yield a high cognitive load because learners must deal with several elements simulta- neously. The only way to foster understanding and to reduce intrinsic cognitive load is to develop schemas that incorporate the interacting elements. It follows that a large number of interacting elements for one person might be included within a single element for another more experienced person who already has a schema that incorporates the elements. Thus, ele- ment interactivity can be estimated only by counting the number of interacting elements dealt with by people at a particular level of expertise. By contrast with intrinsic load, extraneous load is imposed by instructional procedures. Overloading one of the processors that constitute working memory may also increase it. Visual and auditory working memory are partially independent. If multiple sources of information that are required for understanding are all presented in visual form (e.g. a written text and a diagram), they are more likely to overload the visual processor than if the written material is presented in spoken form, thus enabling some of the cognitive load to be shifted to the auditory processor. 13 Germane load, ﬁnally, refers to the working memory resources used to deal with intrinsic cognitive load, which lead to learning. For instance, learners con- struct schemas that deal with the interacting elements associated with intrinsic cognitive load by working on a series of tasks and abstracting away from them by identifying structural features and surface features in a process of induction or ‘mindful abstraction’. They also construct schemas when they connect new information elements to the things they already know, that is, to existing schemas in long-term memory, in a process of elaboration. These processes of dealing with intrinsic cognitive load include elements related to previous tasks or to knowledge already available in long-term memory and thus require working memory resources that correspond to a germane cognitive load that is directly relevant for learning. Cognitive load theory assumes that intrinsic and extraneous cognitive loads are additive. Whether extraneous load presents students with a problem depends, in part, on the intrinsic load. If intrinsic load is low, a high extraneous load resulting from an inadequate instructional design may not be harmful because the total cognitive load is within working memory limits. Indeed, research has shown that instruction designed to decrease extraneous load has negligible effects on learning simple tasks (i.e. involving low element-interactive materials 14). There simply is no need to decrease extraneous load because there are sufﬁcient cognitive resources available to deal with the low intrinsic cognitive load. However, for teaching complex tasks (i.e. involving high element-interactive materials), the sum of the intrinsic and extraneous loads may easily surpass working memory capacity and yield overload (Fig. 1a). However, for teaching complex tasks (i.e. involving high element-interactive materials), the sum of the intrinsic and extraneous loads may easily surpass working memory capacity and yield overload (Fig. 1a). Then, extraneous load and, if the reduction of extraneous load is still insufﬁcient, intrinsic load must be lowered to free up processing resources necessary for learning (Fig. 1b). The more extrane- ous cognitive load is reduced, the more working memory resources can be devoted to intrinsic cogni- tive load and so the easier it becomes to induce a germane cognitive load for learning (Fig. 1c). The next section discusses design guidelines for managing cognitive load. DESIGN GUIDELINES Design principles and strategies based on CLT aim to prevent overload and optimise germane load in order to improve learning. The main principles and strategies for decreasing extraneous load, managing intrinsic load and optimising germane load are summarised and illustrated in Table 1. Moreover, they are related to the expertise reversal effect, which indicates that principles that work well for novice learners may not work well or may even have negative effects for more experienced learners. Decreasing extraneous load Sweller et al. 2 reviewed six research-based principles to decrease extraneous load for novice learners. Firstly, the goal-free principle suggests replacing conventional tasks with goal-free tasks, which provide learners with a non-speciﬁc goal (e.g. replace ‘ﬁnd the most probable aetiological explanation for these symp- toms’ with ‘ﬁnd as many aetiological explanations for these symptoms as you can’). If learners are given a speciﬁc goal, they start reasoning from this goal and try to ﬁnd operators that reduce the difference between the goal state and the given state. This backward search process yields a high extraneous load that can be avoided by eliminating a speciﬁc goal that renders working backward from the goal impossible. Secondly, the worked example principle suggests replac- ing conventional tasks with worked examples that must be carefully studied by the learners. Thirdly, the completion principle suggests replacing conventional tasks with completion tasks, which provide a partial solution that must be completed by the learners. Like worked examples, completion tasks reduce extraneous load caused by weak problem-solving methods because giving part of the solution reduces the size of the problem space. Fourthly, the split attention principle recommends replacing multiple sources of information that are distributed in space or time, such as pictures and accompanying text or a piece of equipment and instructions for operating it, with a single, integrated source of information (Fig. 2 ). The integrated information source reduces extraneous load because there is no need for the learners to mentally integrate the information from different sources. Fifthly, the modality principle recommends replacing a written explanatory text and another source of visual information such as a diagram (unimodal) with a spoken explanatory text and the visual source of information (multimodal). Multimodal information presentation reduces extraneous load because it uses both the visual and the auditory processor of working memory and thus, in effect, increases available working memory capacity. Sixthly, the redundancy principle suggests replacing multiple sources of information that are self-con- tained (i.e. they can be understood on their own) with only one source of information. The single source reduces extraneous load that is caused by unnecessarily processing redundant information. Managing intrinsic load For highly complex or ill-deﬁned tasks, even after the removal of all sources of extraneous load, the element interactivity of the materials may still be too high to allow for learning. In such cases it becomes necessary to decrease intrinsic load. However, because intrinsic load is determined by the interac- tion between the nature of the materials being learned and the expertise of the learner, it cannot be altered without reducing learners’ level of under- standing. Multiple-step strategies rather than single-step principles are needed for sequencing materials from low to high element interactivity, so that tasks are presented in their full complexity only in a later learning phase. Pollock et al. 15 presented learners with a simple-to- complex sequence of instruction. In the ﬁrst part, intrinsic load was reduced by not presenting all the information at once. Instead, isolated elements that could be processed serially were presented. In the second part, however, all the information was pre- sented at once, including the interactions among the elements. As hypothesised, although understanding was lower in the ﬁrst phase of instruction when elements were presented in isolation, this deﬁciency was compensated in the second phase when the full set of interacting elements was presented. Thus, presenting the full set of interacting elements in both phases resulted in less understanding than presenting isolated elements in the ﬁrst phase followed by the full set in the second phase. Manipulating the ﬁdelity of the learning environment is another way to gradually increase the number of interacting elements because high-ﬁdelity environ- ments will typically contain more interacting ele- ments than low-ﬁdelity environments. 6 Although students of

Thus, presenting the full set of interacting elements in both phases resulted in less understanding than presenting isolated elements in the ﬁrst phase followed by the full set in the second phase. Manipulating the ﬁdelity of the learning environment is another way to gradually increase the number of interacting elements because high-ﬁdelity environ- ments will typically contain more interacting ele- ments than low-ﬁdelity environments. 6 Although students of medicine, for example, may learn to diagnose ill-deﬁned problems such as chronic low back pain immediately, they should not begin with real patients. It may be better to start with low-ﬁdelity simulations (e.g. textual problems or case descrip- tions of prospective patients), then continue with medium-ﬁdelity simulations (e.g. computer-simulated patients or simulated patients [SPs] played by peer students), continue with high-ﬁdelity simulations (e.g. SPs played by actors), and end with the real environment (e.g. real patients during an internship in hospital; see example 16). Optimising germane load by increasing intrinsic load The reduction of cognitive load prevents overload and frees up processing resources that can be devoted to genuine learning. It is sometimes desir- able to increase intrinsic load in order to increase the associated germane load. Paas and van Merrie ¨nb- oer 17 were the ﬁrst to relate variability of learning tasks to germane load. Variability of task situations encourages learners to construct cognitive schemas because it increases the probability that similar features can be identiﬁed and that relevant features can be distinguished from irrelevant ones. For example, when students learn about acid-base bal- ance, different learning tasks should relate this concept to hyper- and hypoventilation, aspirin over- dosing, loss of ﬁxed acid through excessive vomiting, and so forth. Such exposure to a highly varied sequence of tasks or solutions helps learners deter- mine the range of applicability of constructed schemas. Increasing variability increases intrinsic cognitive load. Students must learn which problems belong to the same or different categories, an important aspect of the task which is ignored under conditions of low variability. Contextual interference is related to variability. It is low if adjacent tasks in a practice schedule rely on exactly the same skills and it is high if adjacent tasks rely on different skills. Van Merrie¨nboer et al. 18 compared a random practice schedule (e.g. BCBAABCCA) with high contextual interference with a blocked practice schedule (e.g. AAABBBCCC) with low contextual interference. A third design principle is related to the so-called self-explanation effect. The intrinsic load and hence the germane load associated with explaining a concept to oneself are far higher than when simply processing the information because the number of interacting elements considered is deliberately in- creased by including prior-knowledge elements from long-term memory. Stark et al. 19 studied learning from worked examples. They found that effective example elaboration is indeed associated with a higher germane load and improves learning outcomes. Expertise reversal effect An interaction effect that is particularly relevant when CLT is applied to the design of programmes with longer duration is the expertise reversal effect (see overview 20). This effect is an interaction between several basic cognitive load effects and level of expertise. The effect is demonstrated when instruc- tional methods that work well for novice learners have no effects or even adverse effects when learners acquire more knowledge. Thus, multiple-step strate- gies are needed to sequence instructional methods in such a way that they take the growing level of expertise of learners into account. Kalyuga et al. 21 demonstrated that, with increasing expertise, the worked example effect ﬁrst disappears and then reverses. Worked examples become redun- dant for more knowledgeable learners and so impose an extraneous load. These ﬁndings suggest that a training programme should ideally start with worked examples and smoothly work up to conventional tasks. Van Merrie¨nboer 22 introduced the completion strategy to reach this goal: the training starts with full worked examples that include all of the solution steps, proceeds with a series of completion tasks that provide fewer and fewer of the required steps, and ends with conventional tasks that require learners to generate all required steps. text: These ﬁndings suggest that a training programme should ideally start with worked examples and smoothly work up to conventional tasks. Van Merrie¨nboer 22 introduced the completion strategy to reach this goal: the training starts with full worked examples that include all of the solution steps, proceeds with a series of completion tasks that provide fewer and fewer of the required steps, and ends with conventional tasks that require learners to generate all required steps. Recent research indicates that the ﬁrst phase can be further divided into one sub-phase in which students work on process-oriented worked examples and a second sub-phase in which they work on product-oriented examples. 23 Renkl and Atkinson 24 and Atkinson et al.25 reviewed studies that applied the completion strategy or alternative fading guidance procedures, where lear- ner support and guidance decreased as learners acquired more expertise. They concluded that both the completion strategy and other fading guidance strategies are effective to manage cognitive load throughout the various phases of skill acquisition and yield higher learning outcomes than the traditional use of example-problem pairs. The expertise reversal effect has also been found for the split attention principle and the modality princi- ple. Kalyuga et al. 26 demonstrated the usual split attention effect with novice learners. As levels of expertise increased, the advantage of the integrated conditions ﬁrst disappeared and eventually reversed with the separate condition being superior to the integrated condition. The text had become redun- dant for experienced learners. Kalyuga et al. 27 found that among novices, dual mode, auditory and visual presentations were superior to visual-only presenta- tions, demonstrating the modality effect. With more experience, the auditory component became redundant and was best eliminated. CONCLUSIONS This article presents the cognitive architecture assumed by CLT and the main design guidelines that have been developed over the last 20 years. Because there is a close association between guidelines and cognitive architecture, we believe that applications of CLT yield effective instruction that is compatible with human cognitive processing. A rigorous testing programme, based on replicated and controlled experimental studies, has been characteristic of CLT. Current research in CLT concerns various questions related, for example, to the measurement of cognitive load, 28,29 adaptive instruction30 and self-directed learning.31 Each of these research directions, along with many others, has the potential to change and improve CLT. Strohmaier a , b , * , Timo Ehmke b , c , Hendrik H ¨artig b , d , Dominik Leiss b , e a Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Social Sciences and Technology, Department of Educational Sciences, Munich, Germany b Leuphana University of Lüneburg, Center for Empirical Research on Language and Education, Lüneburg, Germany c Leuphana University of Lüneburg, Institute of Educational Sciences, Lüneburg, Germany d University of Duisburg-Essen, Department of Physics Education, Essen, Germany e Leuphana University of Lüneburg, Institute of Mathematics and its Didactics, Lüneburg, Germany ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Language Text comprehension STEM Cohesion Coherence ABSTRACT Learning from texts is an important part of STEM education, but linguistic text features can affect comprehension and learning. We synthesized 45 experimental studies that investigated the effect of linguistic modifications on STEM text comprehension and learning, with a total of N = 6477 learners. In a meta-regression, we distinguished between eight categories of linguistic modifi - cations and several other moderators, including prior knowledge. We found a small positive mean effect of linguistic modifications ( g = 0.15). In line with previous research, the results showed that learners with low content prior knowledge benefited more from linguistic modifications. Personalization and increasing clarity and elaboration had positive effects, while reducing complexity and increasing cohesion did not have significant effects. This study highlights the potential and limits of linguistic modifications in STEM texts and provides implications for educational practice. 1. Introduction Texts are important in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) 1 education in schools and universities ( Schleppegrell, 2007 ; van den Broek, 2010 ). Comprehending texts is a complex cognitive task that is influenced by the linguistic features of the text and various aspects of the reader ( McNamara & Magliano, 2009 ). STEM texts in particular present content-related challenges but also unique linguistic features that make them difficult to understand for many readers ( Best et al., 2005 ; Cruz Neri & Retelsdorf, 2022 ; Goldman & Bisanz, 2002 ; van den Broek et al., 2002 ). To design good texts for STEM education, it is important to understand how changes to linguistic features, which we refer to as linguistic modifications , can positively impact comprehension and learning for particular groups of learners. Previous research has adressed this question by systematically investigating effects of linguistic modifications of STEM texts on comprehension and learning outcomes.

Moreover, it has been shown that individual characteristics interact with linguistic features, and that therefore, a lingusitic modification might be helpful for one group of learners, but not for the other (Best et al., 2005; McNamara et al., 1996). This makes it difficult for researchers and practitioners to decide whether and how to linguistically modify STEM texts for their specific purpose (Cruz Neri & Retelsdorf, 2022). In the present study, we adressed this issue by conducting a meta-analysis on the effects of linguistic modifications on compre - hension and learning from STEM texts. By simultaneously including several linguistic modifications in a meta-regressional approach, we isolated the unique contributions of each modification. Moreover, we included various characteristics of the studies and their samples in order to identify factors that moderated the effectiveness of linguistic modifications. This study aims to provide guidance for researchers and educators from STEM disciplines to construct, analyze and modify texts for optimal learning and comprehension. This goal reflects the long-standing call to summarize research findings from research on text comprehension in a way that allows teachers from non-linguistic disciplines to implement them in their classrooms in order to provide their students with optimal support and appropriate assessment (e.g., Fang et al., 2008; Hand et al., 2010; Snow, 2002). In the following sections, we provide an overview of the process of text comprehension and learning from texts and outline the specific characteristics and challenges of reading STEM texts. We review studies that aimed to improve STEM texts for comprehension and learning, suggesting a categorization of linguistic modifications. Additionally, we review the role of prior knowledge before summarizing open questions and outlining the goals of this study. 1.1. Comprehension and learning from texts 1.1.1. Models of text comprehension Text comprehension is the process of constructing a mental representation of a text, capturing its elements and their semantic relations (Goldman & Bisanz, 2002; van den Broek et al., 2002; see McNamara & Magliano, 2009, for a review). The terms situation model (van Dijk & Kintsch, 1983) or knowledge structure (Follmer et al., 2018) describe concepts similar to mental representations, but with nuanced differences. The process of building the mental representation involves (1) interpreting the meaning of words and larger linguistic units of the text, (2) determining their semantic connections, and (3) relating it to other information, such as prior knowledge or preceding sentences (van den Broek et al., 2002). The resulting mental representation is unique to each reader (Schnotz & Bannert, 2003) and contains information that is directly retrieved from the text, but also information that is added by the reader (McNamara & Magliano, 2009). Therefore, individual characteristics and cognitive resources will influence the processes and the products of text compre - hension (Cromley & Azevedo, 2007; Retelsdorf et al., 2011). The decoding of words and the semantic mapping of elements of the text with each other and with prior knowledge is mostly automatic, but conscious inferences may be necessary if automatic mapping is not successful. This requires the availability of cognitive resources such as working memory capacity (Bohn-Gettler & Kendeou, 2014; Kintsch & van Dijk, 1978) and executive functions (Butterfuss & Kendeou, 2017; Follmer & Sperling, 2018) and can be related to Cognitive Load Theory (Ozuru et al., 2009). 1

Comprehension and learning In the present study, we refer to learning as the “incorporation of comprehended information into the reader’s background knowledge” (van den Broek, 2010, p. 453). This narrow definition is limited to the content of the text as the learning object. In reality, students can arguably learn more from a STEM text than just its content, which is not the focus of this paper. Comprehension and learning are intertwined during the reading of STEM texts. In theory, text comprehension finishes with a mental representation, and learning (in this narrow sense) begins when comprehended information is integrated with the readers’ knowledge base. Thus, per definition, comprehension precedes learning. However, it practically impossible to distinguish between the two: On the one hand, the process of text comprehension constantly relates prior knowledge and information from the text and has the potential to thereby expand and modify the reader’s knowledge base (McNamara & Magliano, 2009). On the other hand, the process of learning will include revisiting aspects of the text and comprehend it again. Therefore, we use the term comprehension and learning in the current paper and refer to all aspects of the construction of a mental representation from a text and its integration with the reader’s knowledge base. Within this terminology, we distinguish three levels of comprehension and learning based on the tasks that are used for assessment: recall, application, and transfer (McNamara & Magliano, 2009). Recall tasks assess the ability to reproduce explicit textual information. They require superficial comprehension and some learning in the form of memorization, but no integration with prior knowledge. Application tasks require the reader to process the comprehended information, for example, by making inferences, which makes it more likely that the content of the text has been integrated with prior knowledge. Finally, transfer tasks require the integration of the comprehended information with the readers knowledge base, which indicates deeper comprehension and learning. 1.1.3. Comprehension and learning from STEM texts STEM texts present specific challenges in text comprehension compared to other types of texts, which can be structured according to the three processes of building a mental representation (1) interpreting elements of the text (2) determining semantic connections across elements, and (3) relating it with prior knowledge (see Sect. 1.1.1; van den Broek et al., 2002). Educational Research Review 39 (2023) 100533 3 (1) STEM texts are particularily challenging regarding word decoding and concept building, even for proficient readers ( Deese, 1962 ; Fang et al., 2006 ; Follmer et al., 2018 ). Process models of text comprehension typically focus less on lower-level processes like word decoding ( McNamara & Magliano, 2009 , but see Cromley et al., 2010 , for a counterexample) but STEM texts frequently use technical vocabulary and academic language, which are more difficult to decode, trigger fewer background knowledge and spread less cognitive activation ( Best et al., 2005 ; Graesser et al., 2011 ; Schleppegrell, 2001 ; Snow & Uccelli, 2009 ). In addition, STEM texts often have a complex syntax, which makes it more difficult to parse sentences and extract meaning, and adds demands on readers ’ working memory by increasing the information required to be processed simulta - neously ( Best et al., 2005 ; Graesser et al., 2011 ). (2) Determining the semantic connections between elements of the text is particularily challenging for STEM texts because they are typically informational or expository texts with a logical semantic structure, which is harder to comprehend than the linear temporal structure of basic narrative texts ( Cot ´e et al., 1998 ; Follmer et al., 2018 ; Graesser et al., 2002 ; van den Broek, 2010 ; Weaver & Kintsch, 1991 ). This makes it more difficult to establish semantic links and construct mental representations of STEM texts. (3) STEM texts are challenging in terms of inferring the relation between the text and prior knowledge ( Ozuru et al., 2009 ). Their purpose in educational settings is often to teach complex, new knowledge and unknown concepts or to assess such knowledge, which is often unfamiliar, difficult to map, and may even conflict with prior knowledge ( van den Broek, 2010 ; Tippett, 2010 ; Weaver & Kintsch, 1991 ). This makes STEM texts notoriously hard to understand as text comprehension heavily relies on activating and using prior knowledge to build inferences ( Best et al., 2005 ; Cromley et al., 2010 ; Follmer et al., 2018 ). 1

STEM text comprehension and cognitive load theory Because working memory is an important resource in reading, Cognitive Load Theory can be used to describe how linguistic features and characteristics of the reader can influence comprehension and learning from STEM texts ( Paas et al., 2003 ; Sweller, 1994 ; Sweller et al., 2019 ; see also Kintsch & van Dijk, 1978 ). Cognitive Load Theory divides cognitive load into three categories: intrinsic , extraneous , and germane . These categories compete for limited working memory capacity 2 . In reading STEM texts, intrinsic load is related to the inherent complexity of the STEM content and is lower for students with higher content prior knowledge ( Sweller et al., 2019 ; van Merri ¨enboer & Sweller, 2005 ). Extraneous load refers to cognitive processes that are irrelevant for successful comprehension and learning. Among other factors, it can potentially be influenced by the design of the text: Linguistic complexity of STEM texts can be considered extraneous load because it requires working memory capacity but does not, by itself, contribute to the building of a mental representation ( Mikk, 2008 ). Germane load is the necessary and desirable cognitive load for comprehension and learning. All three aspects of cognitive load are relevant for supporting comprehension and learning from STEM texts: If prior knowledge is higher, intrinsic load might be reduced, supporting knowledge construction ( Sweller et al., 2019 ; van Merri ¨enboer & Sweller, 2005 ). By reducing extraneous load, cognitive resources for germane load are freed up ( Mikk, 2008 ) and effective learning environment design and promoting effective reading strategies can further enhance germane load ( Leutner et al., 2009 ; Sweller et al., 1998 ). 1.2. Improving STEM texts for learning and comprehension with lingusitic modifications Previous research has aimed to improve comprehension and learning from STEM texts by modifying linguistic features which targeted one or more of the three steps in the process of building a mental representation (see Sect. 1.1.1). Accordingly, we propose to classify linguistic modifications in three categories: The first category are modifications which support the reader in interpreting the meaning of text elements by reducing linguistic complexity . This should make the process of decoding easier ( McNamara & Magliano, 2009 ) and reduce extraneous cognitive load ( Mikk,

text: learning from STEM texts by modifying linguistic features which targeted one or more of the three steps in the process of building a mental representation (see Sect. 1.1.1). Accordingly, we propose to classify linguistic modifications in three categories: The first category are modifications which support the reader in interpreting the meaning of text elements by reducing linguistic complexity . This should make the process of decoding easier ( McNamara & Magliano, 2009 ) and reduce extraneous cognitive load ( Mikk, 2008 ). The second category are modifications that make semantic links of elements within a text more explicit (i.e., increasing cohesion 3 ). This aims at making it easier for the reader to establish a connected mental representation and decreasing the amount of information that has to be kept in the working memory, also decreasing cognitive load ( van den Broek, 2010 ). The third category are modifications that support the reader in integrating prior knowledge with the infor - mation from the text by increasing clarity and elaborations . These three categories may overlap; for example, more common words are easier to decode but will also spread activation more strongly, which helps the reader to infer semantic links ( Graesser et al., 2011 ). Conversely, the categories may also contradict each other: Connecting sentences to increase cohesion simultaniously increases syn - tactic complexity. In line with previous research (e.g., Cruz Neri & Retelsdorf, 2022 ; McNamara & Magliano, 2009 ), we propose to further distinguish between local linguistic modifications like words or propositions within a sentence and global linguistic modifications which refer to the text and its content as a whole. This two-dimensional distinction leads to a 2 × 3 matrix of categories of linguistic modifications which is given in Table 1 . Reducing word-level complexity Word-level complexity was decreased by replacing less frequent words with more frequent words ( Arya et al., 2011 ; Plath, 2020 ; Wenger & Spyridakis, 1993 ), longer words with shorter words, or technical vocabulary with more general terms ( Burton, 2014 ). Because technical vocabulary might be part of the learning content, other studies only simplified non-technical terms ( H ¨artig et al., 2019 ; Williams, 1968 ). Complex grammatical structures on the word level like compounds, nominalizations, appositives or derivatives were also avoided ( Arya et al., 2011 ; H ¨artig et al., 2019 ; Plath, 2020 ; Wenger & Spyridakis, 1993 ). These studies did not demonstrate clear unique effects of decreasing word-level complexity on comprehension and learning, since only two studies modified word-level complexity without, at the same time, also varying other linguistic aspects. These studies re - ported mixed results ( Arya et al., 2011 ; Burton, 2014 ). 1.2.2. Reducing syntactic complexity Syntactic complexity was reduced by shortening sentences ( Burton, 2014 ; Hacker et al., 1992 ; Ikeda & Kitagami, 2013 ; Walkington et al., 2017 ), splitting up subordinate and main clauses ( Hacker et al., 1992 ; H ¨artig et al., 2019 ; Wenger & Spyridakis, 1993 ), or by simplifying the syntax ( Arya et al., 2011 ; Meneses et al., 2018 ; Plath, 2020 ; Schneider et al., 2018 ). Two studies reduced the use of passive voice ( Plath, 2020 ; Wenger & Spyridakis, 1993 ). Only Walkington et al. (2017) analyzed the effect of sytactic complexity in isolation and did not find a significant effect on comprehension. 1.2.3. Increasing local cohesion Cohesion refers to the clarity of semantic, referential, causal, temporal or spatial ties of elements within a text. Local cohesion refers to the connection within and between consecutive sentences and sentences in close proximity ( McNamara & Magliano, 2009 , van Dijk & Kintsch, 1983 ). Local cohesion is typically improved either by increasing referential overlap between sentences or by signaling the connections between sentences with connectives. Local cohesion is typically improved either by increasing referential overlap between sentences or by signaling the connections between sentences with connectives. Increasing referential overlap was achieved by using of the same terms repeatedly instead of replacing them with synonyms ( Boscolo & Mason, 2003 ; Deppert, 2001 ; Follmer & Sperling, 2018 ; Hall et al., 2016 ; H ¨artig et al., 2019 ; Meneses et al., 2018 ; Schneider et al., 2018 ). Similarly, avoiding unspecific pronouns and repeating explicit nouns is assumed to increase cohesion ( Degand et al., 1999 ; Gasparinatou & Grigoriadou, 2010 , 2011 , 2013 ; Hall et al., 2014 ; Hall et al., 2015 ; Ikeda & Kitagami, 2013 ; Kamalski et al., 2008 ; McNamara, 2001 ; McNamara et al., 2011 ; O ’ Reilly & McNamara, 2007 ; Ozuru et al., 2010 ; Ozuru et al., 2009 ; Wittwer & Ihme, 2014 ). The overlap between sentences was increased by using similar phrases and words for similar concepts across the text ( Ikeda & Kitagami, 2013 ; McNamara, 2001 ; McNamara et al., 2011 ; O ’ Reilly & McNamara, 2007 ; Ozuru et al., 2010 ; Ozuru et al., 2009 ). No studies investigated the effect of increasing referential overlap in isolation, so the individual effect of this modification is unclear. Local cohesion was also improved by using connectives , which are words or phases that serve the function of logically connecting sentences or clauses (e.g., Degand et al., 1999 ). Increasing global clarity and elaboration Apart from elaborations within a sentence, elaborations and clarity can also be increased on a global text level. This was done by including summarizing headings and subheadings, previews, thematic sentences, and macropropositions which direct the attention to the core ideas from the text ( Boscolo & Mason, 2003 ; Gasparinatou & Grigoriadou, 2010 , 2011 ; Kamalski et al., 2008 ; McNamara, 2001 ; McNamara et al., 1996 ; McNamara et al., 2011 ; O ’ Reilly & McNamara, 2007 ; Ozuru et al., 2009 ; Schneider et al., 2018 ; Spyridakis & Standal, 1987 ; Wenger & Spyridakis, 1993 ). Other studies made headings more concrete ( Lippmann et al., 2019 ), added summaries that repeated core information from the text ( Vidal-Abarca & Sanjose, 1998 ), added advance organizers or organizational signals that elaborated on the text structure ( Gasparinatou & Grigoriadou, 2010 ; Kamalski et al., 2008 ; S ´anchez et al., 2017 ; Wenger & Spyridakis, 1993 ) or explicitly stated a top-level structure ( Meyer et al., 1980 ). Studies which investigated such modifications in isolation reported mixed results, including substantial differences based on prior knowledge ( Boscolo & Mason, 2003 ; Gasparinatou & Grigoriadou, 2010 ; McNamara et al., 1996 ), inconclusive results ( Gasparinatou & Grigoriadou, 2011 ; Spyridakis & Standal, 1987 ) or no effects ( Lippmann et al., 2019 ). Personalization aims to increase readers ’ elaboration of the text by increasing involvement, motivation, and engagement, for example, by using second person personal pronouns and possessive pronouns instead of definite articles ( Cordova & Lepper, 1996 ; Ginns et al., 2013 ). Three studies investigated the effect of personalization on learning from STEM texts ( Dutke et al., 2016 ; Moreno & Mayer, 2000 ; Stiller & Jedlicka, 2010 ), which all addressed the effect in isolation. Prior knowledge and linguistic modifications Apart from investigating the effects of linguistic modifications, previous research on text comprehension has tried to identify moderating characteristics of readers that determine if such modifications affect comprehension and learning or not (e.g., McNamara et al., 1996 ; McNamara & Kintsch, 1996 ). Because processes of comprehension and learning largely involve an interaction between the text and the reader ( Cromley & Azevedo, 2007 ), individual differences are likely to occur ( Best et al., 2005 ). Thus, the optimal text modification might depend on the prior knowledge of the reader, both with regard to the content domain and to language ( van den Broek, 2010 ). 1.3.1. Content prior knowledge Various studies by McNamara and colleagues found that increasing text cohesion helps students with lower prior knowledge, but is substantially less benefitial for high prior knowledge students (e.g., McNamara, 2001 ; McNamara et al., 1996 ; McNamara & Kintsch, 1996 ; McNamara et al., 2011 ; Ozuru et al., 2009 , but see also O ’ Reilly & McNamara, 2007 , for opposite findings). This is known as the reverse cohesion effect ( McNamara et al., 1996 ; O ’ Reilly & McNamara, 2007 ). More generally, this phenomenon can be understood as a specific case of an expertise reversal effect ( Kalyuga et al., 2003 ; Ozuru et al., 2009 ) and could also affect lingusitic modifictaions other than increasing cohesion. Possibly, lingusitic modifications might help some readers to tackle difficult texts, but could hinder self-directed cognitive activities for others ( Wittwer & Renkl, 2008 ). Few studies have specifically adressed the expertise reversal effect beyond cohesion or particularly from a perspective of learning from STEM texts ( Best et al., 2005 ; Follmer & Sperling, 2018 ). The effect might be stronger in STEM texts as content prior knowledge is important for comprehension, and students differ greatly in prior STEM knowledge ( Alexander et al., 1994

The present study Previous research has found that modifying linguistic features of STEM texts can impact comprehension and learning. However, the results of these studies are inconsistent and make it difficult for researchers and practitioners to determine effective modifications. This is due to: (1) Studies usually addressing multiple modifications at once, with few studies utilizing linguistic modifications in isolation, making it unclear which particular modification was effective; (2) the use of different texts from study to study, so that the same linguistic modification might be differently effective in one text or the other (Follmer et al., 2018); (3) small sample sizes in some studies, leading to many inconclusive results. (4) the potentially differential effectiveness for different groups of learners (e.g., McNamara et al., 1996) which limits transferability of results. These difficulties lead to a situation where substantial evidence has been gathered throughout recent decades, but still without a clear conclusion on which particular linguistic modifications improve learning with STEM texts, and for which group of learners. In the present study, we approached this gap by combining existing studies in a meta-analytical aproach to adressing the following research questions. (1) What is the overall effect of linguistic modifications on comprehension and learning from STEM texts? (2)

In the present study, we approached this gap by combining existing studies in a meta-analytical aproach to adressing the following research questions. (1) What is the overall effect of linguistic modifications on comprehension and learning from STEM texts? (2) How do content prior knowledge and language prior knowledge moderate the effect of linguistic modifications on compre - hension and learning from STEM texts? (3) Which categories of linguistic modifications (reducing complexity, increasing internal links, and increasing links with prior knowledge) at both local and global levels improve comprehension and learning from STEM texts? (4) Which other study characteristics (assessment outcome, publication year, domain, text length, text language, age group, study location) moderate the effect of linguistic modifications on comprehension and learning from STEM texts? 3. Methods 3.1. Study selection Relevant studies were identified by database searches and cross-reference checks. Database searches were conducted in Web of Science, Scopus, PSYNDEX, ProQuest and FIS Bildung, including studies published up to and including 2020. Approximately 50 search terms referring to text characteristics, outcome, STEM and material were used (see Table A.1). The database search resulted in 1525 hits (excluding duplicates). Abstracts were screened independently by a subset of two of the four authors. If they disagreed, an independent screening was done by a third author based on the same criteria. The inclusion criteria were. 1) The study used a linguistic modification of a text. We did not include studies that focused only on variations of the content or structural level. For example, we did not include studies implementing a refutational structure (see Tippett, 2010, for an overview), or studies investigating the effect of seductive details (see Sundararajan & Adesope, 2020, for a meta-analysis), since the mech - anisms behind these modifications are arguably not based primarily on linguistic processes. 2) The study included an experimental design with at least two groups or conditions regarding linguistic modifications. 3) The study reported a measure of text comprehension or achievement as an outcome variable, and this measure was the same for all experimental groups. 4) The manipulated text covered STEM or science topics (based on the description of these domains in Graesser et al., 2002). 5) The study used linear, written texts (no hypertexts or websites). This could include digital texts, but only if the structure was similar to printed texts. 6) The study was written in English or German, but the texts used could be in any language. Based on this screening, 77 studies were categorized as possibly relevant by both screeners,

Based on this screening, 77 studies were categorized as possibly relevant by both screeners, 1364 were categorized as irrelevant. 84 cases resulted in a disagreement (70 of them regarding Criterium 1), in 31 of these cases the third coder decided to include the studies. This resulted in a total of 108 possibly relevant studies, which were retrieved as full texts. These full texts were again screened based on the same criteria by the first author and the inclusion of each study was discussed by all four authors. In contrast to the first screening, this also included information from the full text, including details of the design and topic of the texts, the outcome measures, and the statistical design. This led to the exclusion of 70 studies. Finally, 38 studies were selected and 9 additional studies were included through cross-reference searches within all screened full texts. In cases where the reported information was not sufficient for coding, authors of the studies were contacted. In two cases, the missing information could not be retreived and the studies were excluded from the dataset. Ultimately, 45 studies were included for analyses. A.R. Strohmaier et al. A detailed coding sheet was created for the coding process. For the coding of lingusitic modifications, the process included an explorative phase and a validation phase with double-coding by two authors (see Section 5.2.3 ). All other variables were coded only by the first author. 3.2.1. Linguistic modifications Initial coding of linguistic modifications was based on the 2 × 3 matrix described in Section 2 . During the explorative coding phase, two of the six categories were split, resulting in a total of eight categories: The category local cohesion was split into overlap and connectives . The category increasing global clarity and elaboration was split into summaries and personalization. Based on the resulting eight categories a detailed coding scheme was created (see Table A.2 ). Each linguistic modification was dummy coded in all eight categories ( yes = 1, no = 0). 4 Two authors then individually coded all linguistic modifications according to the coding scheme, resulting in an agreement of κ = 0.84. Prior knowledge Language-specific and content prior knowledge were categorized as low ( = -1), regular ( = 0), or high ( = 1), respectively. The descriptions of samples in the original studies were used as criteria for this categorization. If a study distinguished between two groups by splitting it based on language-specific or content prior knowledge, they were coded as high and low ; if there was only one group, it was coded as regular , if not specifically characterized otherwise (e.g., in Gasparinatou & Grigoriadou, 2011 ). 3.2.3. Study descriptors To characterize the level of comprehension and learning that studies assessed as outcome measures, we distinguished assessment outcomes in three categories: Recall measures referred to a verbatim reproduction of text-based information (e.g., number of correctly recalled propositions in a free recall task, Boscolo & Mason, 2003 ; or forced-choice fact retreival questions, Wenger & Spyridakis, 1993 ), apply measures referred to questions that could be answered by combining information that was fully given in the text (e.g., bridging-inference questions where information from two separate sentences had to be combined, Gasparinatou & Grigoriadou, 2010 ), transfer measures referred to questions which required information that was not given directly in the text and had to be inferred or taken from prior knowledge (e.g., problem-solving questions, Stiller & Jedlicka, 2010 ; Vidal-Abarca & Sanjose, 1998 ; Wenger & Spyridakis, 1993 ). For 172 extracted effects (91.5%) one of the three categories could be distinctly assigned (78 recall, 66 apply, 28 transfer), while the remaining 16 effects were based on a combination of the assessment types. 28 of the 45 studies (62%) reported effects for outcome measures in more than one category. Model 1 was a standard random-effects model with sampling variance (extracted from the studies) at Level 1 and the random variance of effect sizes at Level 2. For Model 2, we added a third level to account for the nesting of effect sizes within studies. Model 3 included an intermediate level that accounted for the nesting of effect sizes within subgroups, which were in turn nested within studies. Model 4 was a cross-classified random-effects model (CCREM, Fern ´andez-Castilla et al., 2019 ), with assessment type as the cross-level random effect in addition to the hierarchical Levels 2 to 4. For the meta-regression model including linguistic modifications, the intercept was fixed at zero; because all studies were experimental studies, the hypothetical absence of any modification would necessarily lead to a null effect. Thus, in cases were studies included several linguistic modifications, effects of these modifications add up to the total estimated effect. All models were fitted using the R package metafor ( Viechtbauer, 2010 ). Confidence intervals of all estimates were calculated based on a t -distribution, similar to the Knapp and Hartung adjustment ( Knapp & Hartung, 2003 ; Viechtbauer, 2010 ). I 2 (representing the proportion of variation due to heterogeneity) was calculated according to the method described in Viechtbauer (2022 ; see also Cheung, 2014 ; Higgins & Thompson, 2002 ). R 2 values were calculated as described in Cheung (2014) . Tests for residual heterogeneity and omnibus tests of moderators were based on F-distributions ( Viechtbauer, 2010 ). 4. Results 4.1. Publication bias According to Rodgers and Pustejovsky (2020) , existing standard procedures to check for publication bias (including analyses of funnel plot asymmetry, trim-and-fill analyses, or Egger ’ s regression, see Borenstein et al., 2009 ) do not give reliable results for multilevel meta-analyses. An alternative approach is to compare the mean effect size of non-reviewed grey literature against peer-reviewed publications ( Borenstein et al., 2009 ). In our dataset, only two studies were not published in peer reviewed papers, so a systematic comparison by this criterion was not meaningful. Instead, we isolated publications that were either grey literature or did not report a main effect of a linguistic modification in the abstract. Our rationale was that studies that did not focus on the linguistic modification would, similar to grey literature, not be subject to a systematic selection based on the effect size of this modification. Of the 45 studies, 15 did not refer to a main effect of linguistic modification in their abstract or had not been subject to peer-review. The mean effect size in these studies ( g = 0.11) did not differ significantly from the mean effect size reported in the peer-reviewed studies ( g = 0.16), F (1,186) = 0.411, p = .522. Thus, we did not find evidence for a publication bias. 5. Discussion In this meta-analysis, we summarized empirical research findings on the effect of linguistic modifications of STEM texts on comprehension and learning. Regarding our first research question, we found a small overall effect of g = 0.15. Even though linguistically modified texts led to better comprehension and learning in most cases, the size of the average effect indicates that this improvement was not particularly strong compared to other approaches, such as providing feedback ( g = 0.35; Swart et al., 2019 ) or including graphics ( g = 0.39; Guo et al., 2020 ). Linguistic modifications in STEM texts are relevant, but not a guarantee for strong improvements in comprehension and learning. 5.1. Moderators of the effect of linguistic modifications 5.1.1. In the case of linguistic modifications, the expertise reversal effect refers to the idea that readers with low content prior knowledge benefit from linguistic modifications, while the modifications could lose their effectiveness or even have negative effects for readers with high content prior knowledge. The content of STEM texts can be very demanding ( Alexander et al., 1994 ; Best et al., 2005 ; Follmer & Sperling, 2018 ), and there can be large differences in prior knowledge among readers ( Graesser et al., 2002 ), which could mean that the effect is particularly strong for STEM texts. Our meta-analysis allowed us to quantify this effect across all included studies and all linguistic modifications: For low prior- knowledge readers, the mean effect size of linguistic modifications was substantial ( g = 0.35), whereas for high prior knowledge groups, it was almost zero ( g =  0.01). This strongly supports the existence of an expertise reversal effect. However, it should be emphasized that linguistic modifications did not have a relevant negative effect for any readers. There are several possible explanations for this effect. McNamara et al. (1996) suggested that high prior knowledge students process texts only superficially when they do not offer them challenging gaps in cohesion, which could negatively impact compre - hension and learning. According to Cognitive Load Theory, lower prior knowledge might lead to higher intrinsic load ( Sweller et al., 2019 ; van Merri ¨enboer & Sweller, 2005 ), and limit germane load, which is something that linguistic modifications aiming at reducing extraneous load (e.g., by decreasing linguistic complexity) can possibly compensate for. Inducing germane load (e.g., by making the text more explicit or adding elaborations) might be redundant or even have negative effect by misdirecting attention or decreasing engagement ( Kalyuga et al., 2003 ; McNamara et al., 1996 ). Future studies could further consider the role of cognitive load during reading of STEM texts, providing a clearer explanation which processes during comprehension and learning from texts are affected by linguistic modifications, and their relation to prior knowledge. 5.1.2. Language prior knowledge Our meta-analysis did not show an interaction of language prior knowledge with the effect of linguistic modifications. Possibly, this interaction is more complex and depends on other factors which were not considered in our analyses. For example, Ozuru et al. (2009) and O ’ Reilly and McNamara (2007) suggested a three-way interaction between language prior knowledge, content prior knowledge, and assessment type. Another explanation might be that the groups compared here did not differ enough regarding their language prior knowledge. Linguistic modifications might be particularly beneficial for readers with very low language prior knowledge which struggle with basic reading processes, but similarly effective for readers above a certain level. In the studies included in this analysis, readers with low language prior knowledge were usually identified through percentiles or median splits, but the overall level of these groups was not specified. Only two studies used norms of standardized test scores to identify low language prior knowledge ( Geva & Ryan, 1985 ; Meyer et al., 1980 ), and only one study ( Degand & Sanders, 2002 ) compared first and second language learners. Therefore, it is possible that in the studies included here, the language prior knowledge of

text: analysis, readers with low language prior knowledge were usually identified through percentiles or median splits, but the overall level of these groups was not specified. Only two studies used norms of standardized test scores to identify low language prior knowledge ( Geva & Ryan, 1985 ; Meyer et al., 1980 ), and only one study ( Degand & Sanders, 2002 ) compared first and second language learners. Therefore, it is possible that in the studies included here, the language prior knowledge of the participants was not low enough to interact with linguistic modifications, that relevant subgroups were not identified by the applied procedures, or that ouranalytical design did not account for relevant interactions. 5.1.3. Categories of linguistic modifications Regarding research question three, we studied the individual impact of eight categories of linguistic modifications on compre - hension and learning. Previous studies often modified multiple linguistic features simultaneously, making it difficult to compare re - sults ( Cruz Neri & Retelsdorf, 2022 ). Our analysis included all categories in one meta-regression model, which allowed us to isolate their average effects. Only three categories were found to have a significant impact on comprehension and learning: Increasing clarity and elaboration on the word and sentence level, increasing clarity and elaboration on the global text level, and personalization. All three categories aimed to help readers make inferences and connections to prior knowledge and elaborate on key concepts (see Sect. 2). Both increasing clarity and elaboration locally and globally showed relatively small effects on comprehension and learning, but for studies combining these modifications the influence adds up to a moderate-sized effect ( g = 0.35). In contrast to the other modifi - cations, studies that increased clarity and elaboration took into account the content of the text and typically added content information ( McNamara et al., 2010 ). In some studies, this increased text length by up to 50% (e.g., McNamara et al., 1996 ; McNamara et al., 2011 ; Ozuru et al., 2009 ; Vidal-Abarca & Sanjose, 1998 ) or even 100% ( Gasparinatou & Grigoriadou, 2011 ). Thus, it is important to critically discuss the line between linguistic modification and content modification. Our categorization considered the modifications to be linguistic in nature, since the amount of information regarding the target content (which should be comprehended and learned and which was assessed afterwards) remained constant while the sorrounding text was changed to foster comprehension and learning of this content. However, the particular effectiveness of these modifications might indicate that modifications on the linguistic level are generally more helpful when they are interlaced with improvements on the content level. It might be particularly successful to use linguistic modifications for structuring and focusing the reading processes towards the content-specific learning goals. On the local level, this involves clarifying and elabor

text: which should be comprehended and learned and which was assessed afterwards) remained constant while the sorrounding text was changed to foster comprehension and learning of this content. However, the particular effectiveness of these modifications might indicate that modifications on the linguistic level are generally more helpful when they are interlaced with improvements on the content level. It might be particularly successful to use linguistic modifications for structuring and focusing the reading processes towards the content-specific learning goals. On the local level, this involves clarifying and elaborating important aspects of the content. On the global level, content-specific considerations should determine the structure, headings, and content of summaries to maximize comprehension and minimize dis - tractions from irrelevant or redundant information, as shown in research on seductive details ( Sundararajan & Adesope, 2020 ) and the redundancy effect in multimedia learning ( Mayer et al., 2001 ). Personalization of texts had the strongest positive effect in our analyses. This result was based on three studies ( Dutke et al., 2016 ; Moreno & Mayer, 2000 ; Stiller & Jedlicka, 2010 ) which focused only on personalization. This implies a very reliable effect which is clearly attributable to this particular modification. Personalization seems to offer a promising potential for increasing text compre - hension compared to other linguistic modifications. Somewhat surprisingly, the remaining five categories of linguistic modifications did not have a significant effect on comprehension and learning. This finding may be specific to STEM texts, where deeper conceptual understanding is particularly important compared to narrative texts ( van den Broek, 2010 ). In general, the nature of the content of STEM texts might limit the possibilities of linguistic modifications without making concessions to the content. Often, the complexity of the language mirrors the complexity of the content and cannot easily be simplified or changed ( Schleppegrell, 2001 ). For example, the use of technical vocabulary provides difficulties for many readers, but using everyday language is usually not viable for scientific precision. The repeated use of the same words instead of synonyms, which is often considered to increase cohesion and support text comprehension, might be counterproductive when tech - nical terminology is introduced ( van den Broek, 2010 ). Accordingly, some of the approaches to make other texts easier to comprehend might simply not be transferable to STEM texts, or might not address the aspects of the text which are relevant for content-specific comprehension and learning. In addition, Cognitive Load Theory also offers some explanations for the varying effects of the linguistic modifications. It suggests that extraneous load can be reduced by decreasing the cognitive resources that are only required for reading, but not for the processing of the STEM content. For example, increasing cohesion is assumed to reduce the amount of information that has to be kept in working memory in order to infer connections between sentences ( van den Broek, 2010 ). Educational Research Review 39 (2023) 100533 14 effective could indicate that, for the readers included here, the reading process did not cause enough extraneous load to meaningfully interfere with intrinsic and germane load. In contrast, the effective linguistic modifications that aim at increasing links with prior knowledge did not aim at reducing extraneous load, but at directing germane load effectively towards inferences with prior knowledge (see also Leutner et al., 2009 ; Sweller et al., 2019 ; van Merri ¨enboer & Sweller, 2005 ). Possibly for reading STEM texts under regular circumstances and by proficient readers, this could be more effective than freeing up resources by reducing extraneous load. Finally, these analyses are based on a simplified, additive model. Arguably, linguistic features interact which each other, causing more complex interrelations which are not captured by our model. Therefore, future studies might vary different linguistic text fea - tures more systematically, and investigate interactions between them. 5.1.4. Extent of linguistic manipulations In the current meta-analyses, we summarized the effects of original texts versus modified texts without taking the extent of the linguistic modifications into account. The main challenge in quantifying linguistic manipulations is the lack of a common metric. Many studies did not report a metric to quantify their modifications, and if they did, the metrics differed across the categories of linguistic modifications. For example, studies that aimed to increase cohesion often referred to the Coh-Metrix ( Graesser et al., 2011 ), a tool that provides a variety of metrics of text characteristics. Some of these studies reported up to 8 detailed characteristic metrics of their texts (e.g., McNamara et al., 2011 ; Ozuru et al., 2009 ; Ozuru et al., 2010 ). In comparison, studies that modified the use of connectives or simplified words usually reported the absolute number of changes to quantify the modification, or gave specific metrics like the average lexical frequency of the modified words ( Arya et al., 2011 ). Arguably, there is no scientifically reasonable way to compare these values with scores from the Coh-Metrix, which would be necessary in order to include the extent of modifications in a meta-regression as an additional continuous predictor across all modifications. For other modifications like making the top-level structure explicit before the text, it is hard to come up with a way to quantify

text: quantify the modification, or gave specific metrics like the average lexical frequency of the modified words ( Arya et al., 2011 ). Arguably, there is no scientifically reasonable way to compare these values with scores from the Coh-Metrix, which would be necessary in order to include the extent of modifications in a meta-regression as an additional continuous predictor across all modifications. For other modifications like making the top-level structure explicit before the text, it is hard to come up with a way to quantify the changes at all. One common metric, the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL; Flesch, 1948 ; Kincaid et al., 1975 ) was even used for different purposes in different studies. The FKGL takes into account the number of words, sentences, and syllables in a text. In Burton (2014) , the lin - guistic modification aims at increasing readability; therefore, the FKGL was used as a metric to quantify this modification (FKGL (original) ≈ 11.5; FKGL(modified) ≈ 8.9). Follmer and Sperling (2018) aimed at increasing referential cohesion, using FKGL as a control metric to ensure that the modifications did not affect readability (FKGL = 8 in both conditions, see also Lippmann et al., 2019 ). In contrast, increasing cohesion will generally increase the number of words per sentence, which in turn leads to lower readability metrics ( McNamara, 2001 ). Accordingly, studies on cohesion typically reported lower readability metrics after increasing cohesion, for example in O ’ Reilly and McNamara (2007 ; FKGL(low cohesion) = 9.2; FKGL(high cohesion) = 10.5; see also McNamara et al., 2011 ; Ozuru et al., 2010 ; Ozuru et al., 2009 ) In conclusion, meaningfully comparing the extent of linguistic modifications across different categories seems to be hardly possible. Therefore, the reported effects should be understood as averages, and it is possible that some of the modifications could differ in their effect depending on the extent of their implementation. 5.1.5. Expertise reversal effect for specific linguistic modifications We further investigated whether the expertise reversal effect for content prior knowledge differed between the eight categories of linguistic modifications. However, with a total of 16 predictors and the substantial heterogeneity across studies, this analysis should not be overinterpreted. A careful interpretation points towards the finding that the expertise reversal effect for content prior knowledge might differ between linguistic modifications: While increasing personalization and global clarity was significantly more effective for low prior-knowledge groups of participants, no evidence towards the effect was found in the other categories. For lan - guage prior knowledge, no significant interactions were found. Thus, while the possibility of an expertise reversal effect should always be considered when modifying STEM texts, it might

Thus, while the possibility of an expertise reversal effect should always be considered when modifying STEM texts, it might not occur under certain circumstances (see also Follmer & Sperling, 2018 ). 5.1.6. Study characteristics Regarding research question four, we investigated which other study characteristics influenced the effects of linguistic modifications. Our analysis showed no indication that linguistic modifications were more effective for measures of recall, application, or transfer, even though these three measures address different aspects of text comprehension ( McNamara & Magliano, 2009 ). It was notable that many studies primarily assessed measures of recall which often asked for a verbatim reproduction of superficial information from the text. In line with van den Broek (2010) , we found that relatively little research focused on permanent learning. Modifications of physics texts had stronger effects on comprehension and learning than in other domains. However, these texts covered a wide range of topics, contexts, and age groups which makes it difficult to identify a clear explanation. Possibly, the texts that were explicitly situated in physics might have been more demanding. A higher content demand would be equivalent to lower prior knowledge, which could support the success of linguistic modifications. The longer the texts in the summarized studies, the stronger the effect of linguistic modifications were. When very short texts are compared with text of multiple pages, this adds up to a substantial difference, with an increase in effect size of g = 0.017 per 100 words or about g = 0.076 per page. Possibly, longer text put higher demands on cognitive resources, required a more extensive mental representation, and included more distant semantic relations. A.R. Strohmaier et al.
